newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: Paraguayan wheat production seen halved by rain.
newsitem.headline: Paraguayan wheat production seen halved by rain.

text.p: Paraguayan 1996 wheat output has probably been halved by recent torrential rains and imports of Argentine wheat will remain high, the top official from the country's main milling group said Tuesday.

"We calculate that there will be at least 300,000 tonnes of serviceable wheat," Heinz Doll, president of the Paraguayan Chamber of Millers, told Reuters in an interview at the assembly of Latin American millers (ALIM) in Asuncion.
This year's wheat crop is the third in a row which has been devastated by bad weather hitting the harvest, and is a bitter disappointment given the area sown, Doll said.

"Paraguay had the chance this year of achieving its highest ever production. This year we thought they were going to produce at least 600,000 tonnes, when the normal output in Paraguay has been 400,000 to 450,000 tonnes."

Doll said that millers may in the next few years import some higher quality wheat, such as U.S. or Canadian grain, but only if the currently lazy Paraguayan flour market bucks up and starts demanding a better grade of bread products.
Paraguayan flour consumption is stagnant despite a rising population due to competition from mandioca, a starchy vegetable, which has gained ground aided by recent high wheat prices.

Paraguay's over-populated milling industry is in bad financial shape, due partly to demands by small bakeries for under-the-counter sales of flour to avoid tax and also to competition from smuggled Argentine flour.

Only 30 percent of mills are professionally run and can be relied upon to pay their taxes, Doll said. He described how some mills run by cooperatives sold flour on the black market, billing it to their members who under Paraguayan law are exempt from value-added tax.
"There is a joke here that each member of a cooperative is eating at least one tonne of tortillas a day," Doll said.
The government is trying to crack down on the illegal flour trade, but progress is proving slow.

Farmers are waiting for their fields to dry out sufficiently to complete the remaining 50 percent of the harvest, but Doll said he thought most will have gone to ruin. The quality of wheat already harvested is low but acceptable for bread if mixed with better grain.
Last year, Paraguayan farmers produced 300,000 tonnes and wheat imports totaled 150,000 tonnes, all from Argentina.

Argentine wheat faces no serious competition in the Paraguayan import market as millers have to pay a 10 percent tariff on imports from outside the Mercosur customs union and and transport costs from Argentina are only $10 a tonne.
